title: Moment of Inertia of Common Shapes

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

domain: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
expression: I(ring)=MR² ; I(disc/solid cylinder)=½MR² ; I(solid sphere)=(2/5)MR² ; I(hollow sphere)=(2/3)MR² ; I(rod, centre)=(1/12)ML²
explanation: Moment of inertia formulas for standard shapes about their natural symmetry axis, derived by integrating r² dm over the body. Mass distributed FARTHER from the axis (like a ring, all mass at radius R) gives a larger I than mass distributed closer/more toward the centre (like a solid sphere). The parallel axis theorem, I = Icm + Md², lets I about any parallel axis be found from I about the centre-of-mass axis plus Md² (d = distance between the two parallel axes); the perpendicular axis theorem (Iz = Ix + Iy) applies only to PLANAR (2D, lamina) bodies.

variables.meaning: Distance between parallel axes (parallel axis theorem)

workedExample.scenario: A solid sphere of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about an axis through its centre.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the moment of inertia formulas for a solid vs. hollow sphere, or a disc vs. a ring — these differ specifically because of HOW mass is distributed relative to the axis, a very common formula mix-up.
Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to a 3D (non-planar) body — it strictly applies only to flat, lamina (2D) objects.
genZNote: Ring vs. solid disc, same mass and radius — the ring's mass is all camping out at the rim, so it wins on I.
